question: Which physiologic abnormality initiates chronic superficial venous hypertension in the lower extremity?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Incompetent deep or perforating valves permit reflux into the superficial system, producing venous hypertension.
This does not produce the described venous reflux. It would require an arterial process rather than incompetent venous valves.
Sensory nerve dysfunction contributes to neuropathic ulceration, not superficial venous hypertension. Decreased protective sensation would support this mechanism.
Dermal neutrophil influx characterizes pyoderma gangrenosum. A rapidly expanding painful ulcer with a violaceous border would support it.
Sustained pressure contributes to pressure ulcers rather than venous reflux. Immobility with injury over a pressure site would support it.

question: Which lesion is classified as the most important preulcerative finding in a neuropathic foot?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate between venous, arterial and neuropathic dermatologic manifestations (MK1,2 and PCPS5)

options.rationale: Atrophie blanche is associated with fibrotic venous disease. Porcelain-white atrophic scarring would make it appropriate.
Repetitive mechanical forces generate a callus, which is the principal preulcerative lesion in the neuropathic foot.
This pattern suggests early pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid painful expansion after trauma would support that process.
Hemosiderin pigmentation above the medial malleolus supports venous disease. That location and accompanying edema would make it appropriate.
Non-blanchable intact erythema defines a stage I pressure injury. A sacral pressure site with intact skin would support it.

question: Full-thickness skin loss extends into subcutaneous tissue but does not involve the underlying fascia. Which pressure injury stage is present?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing history and physical exam stage a sacral ulcer. (PCPS 2,3,7)

options.rationale: Stage I has intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Intact rather than full-thickness skin would make this correct.
Stage II is partial-thickness loss presenting as an abrasion, blister, or shallow crater. Limited epidermal or dermal loss would support it.
Stage III involves full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue without extension through the underlying fascia.
Stage IV includes destruction involving muscle, bone, tendon, or joint structures. Exposure of those deeper structures would support it.
Impending ulceration corresponds to intact non-blanchable erythema rather than full-thickness loss. Intact skin would make this appropriate.

question: Which examination compares limb pressures to help exclude occlusive disease before external compression?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the ankle / brachial index (ABI) (MK2, PCPS6, SBP5)

options.rationale: Venous duplex documents the presence and cause of venous insufficiency. The requested comparison requires ankle and arm pressures.
Monofilament testing evaluates peripheral neuropathy. Loss of protective sensation rather than concern for arterial occlusion would support it.
Serial measurement and photography document healing response. They do not compare limb pressures or exclude arterial disease.
The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and brachial pressures to screen for arterial occlusive disease before compression.
Reflex testing is part of the neurologic assessment of a leg ulcer. It does not determine whether compression is safe.

question: Chronic venous hypertension causes activated leukocytes to release a fibrogenic mediator. Which tissue change should follow?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Plantar keratin and callus formation relate to repetitive neuropathic pressure. Reduced callus would not explain venous fibrosis.
Neutrophilic dermal influx describes pyoderma gangrenosum. A rapidly progressive undermined ulcer would support that mechanism.
Venous reflux is increased by valvular incompetence. Restored valve function would be needed for reflux to decrease.
Autonomic neuropathy causes loss of sweating and fissuring. Sweat production is not the fibrogenic consequence described.
TGF-β1 promotes collagen production and subcutaneous fibrosis, producing the induration of lipodermatosclerosis.

question: A chronic lower-leg process produces fibrosis that constricts venous and lymphatic channels. Which paired findings best reflect this progression?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Lipodermatosclerosis replaces subcutaneous fat with fibrosis, which can impede venous and lymphatic flow and produce edema above the constriction.
This pairing indicates neuropathic ulcer risk. A plantar pressure point and sensory loss would make it correct.
This pairing indicates arterial insufficiency. A sharply demarcated distal ulcer and low ABI would support it.
This pairing describes a stage II pressure injury. A pressure site with superficial loss would make it correct.
This pairing describes pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid expansion and severe pain would support it.

question: A wound product is applied repeatedly to an ulcer with a disrupted epidermal barrier. Which complication most directly explains worsening inflammation and delayed closure?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Arterial reconstruction failure concerns inadequate restored perfusion. A post-revascularization ischemic wound would be required.
Prolonged exposure to allergenic wound products through a disrupted barrier can cause contact dermatitis and impair healing.
Callus develops from repetitive mechanical pressure in neuropathic feet. A plantar pressure point would support this process.
Valve restoration would reduce rather than worsen venous hypertension. Improved edema after correction would support it.
An open wound increases bacterial entry rather than reducing it. Barrier restoration would be needed for this effect.

question: An ulcer is shallow, irregular, exudative, and located near the medial ankle. Discomfort improves when the limb is raised. Which underlying process best accounts for these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate between venous, arterial and neuropathic dermatologic manifestations (MK1,2 and PCPS5)

options.rationale: Pressure injury follows sustained loading over a pressure site. Immobility and a sacral or other support-surface location would support it.
Neutrophilic inflammation characterizes pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid progression with a violaceous undermined border would support it.
Venous reflux produces hypertension, edema, and the characteristic shallow irregular ulcer near the medial ankle.
Sensory denervation produces unrecognized plantar trauma and callus-associated ulcers. Decreased sensation would be expected.
Arterial hypoperfusion causes sharply demarcated ulcers with minimal exudate and pain that does not improve with elevation.

question: Which combination most strongly favors an arterial ulcer rather than a venous ulcer?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate between venous, arterial and neuropathic dermatologic manifestations (MK1,2 and PCPS5)

options.rationale: These are characteristic venous findings. Their presence with edema and dermatitis would favor venous ulceration.
These findings favor neuropathic ulceration. Decreased sensation and palpable pulses would further support it.
These findings favor a pressure injury. Tissue loss over a sustained pressure site would make that diagnosis appropriate.

options.text: Sharp border and absent pedal pulse
options.rationale: A punched-out sharply defined ulcer with diminished or absent pulses reflects arterial insufficiency.
These findings favor pyoderma gangrenosum. Severe pain and a violaceous edge would further support it.

question: Loss of autonomic function in a neuropathic foot increases infection risk through which sequence?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Autonomic neuropathy causes decreased sweating rather than increased sweating. Persistent moisture from another cause would be required.
This sequence characterizes venous insufficiency. Valvular incompetence with medial ankle pigmentation would support it.
This sequence relates to pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid worsening after trauma would support it.
This sequence reflects peripheral arterial disease. Absent pulses and exertional calf pain would make it appropriate.
Autonomic neuropathy reduces sweating, producing dry cracked skin that creates a portal for bacteria.

question: A clinician suspects that both venous and arterial disease contribute to a lower-leg ulcer. Which finding specifically determines whether high compression can be used?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the ankle / brachial index (ABI) (MK2, PCPS6, SBP5)

options.rationale: Compression is used for venous disease but is avoided when the ABI is below 0.8 because significant arterial disease may coexist.
Failure to shrink after six weeks supports referral, not compression safety. Arterial assessment is still required.
Pigmentation supports venous disease but cannot exclude arterial insufficiency. A safe ABI would still be required.
Callus supports neuropathic pressure injury. It does not establish arterial adequacy for compression.
Contact dermatitis affects wound care but does not determine arterial perfusion. An ABI assessment would be needed.

question: Which pairing correctly links an ulcer type with the mechanism that most directly delays healing?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate between venous, arterial and neuropathic dermatologic manifestations (MK1,2 and PCPS5)

options.rationale: Absent protective sensation is central to neuropathic ulcers. Venous ulcers instead arise from reflux and hypertension.
Arterial disease reduces delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and repair mediators, thereby delaying wound healing.
Superficial venous hypertension causes venous ulcers. Neuropathic ulcers require sensory loss and repetitive pressure or trauma.
Neutrophil influx characterizes pyoderma gangrenosum. Pressure ulcers arise from sustained external loading.
Incompetent perforating valves cause venous hypertension. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic inflammatory process.

question: Which preventive pairing is most appropriate for recurrence after a venous ulcer has healed?
cited_learning_objective: List preventative care for stasis dermatitis and the various forms of leg and sacral ulcers (PCPS 10,11)

options.rationale: Hydrogen peroxide and frequent manipulation can damage tissue. Gentle saline cleansing and less frequent disturbance are preferred.
Topical antibiotics can sensitize the skin, and air exposure is less favorable than a moist environment.
Regular 20-30 mmHg compression stockings help prevent venous re-accumulation and ulcer recurrence after healing.

options.text: Continuous weight bearing and callus retention
options.rationale: These practices increase neuropathic pressure and injury. Off-loading and callus removal would be appropriate for diabetic ulcers.
Trauma can worsen pyoderma gangrenosum through pathergy. This pairing does not prevent venous recurrence.

question: Which osteopathic treatment pairing targets autonomic influence to the lower extremity?
cited_learning_objective: Develop osteopathic treatment plan for blistering, ulcers, and trauma (PCPS 12,13, MK6)

options.rationale: These regions do not match the lower-extremity autonomic levels provided. The specified lower-limb segments would be required.
This pairing does not correspond to the lower-extremity levels presented. T12-L2 and S2-S4 are the relevant targets.
Both segmental ranges differ from those designated for the lower extremity. The lumbar sympathetic and sacral parasympathetic levels are needed.
The lower-extremity plan addresses sympathetic influence at T12-L2 and parasympathetic influence at S2-S4.
These levels fall outside the stated lower-extremity autonomic targets. The designated ranges are T12-L2 and S2-S4.

question: Which intervention pairing most directly supports lymphatic flow in a lower-extremity ulcer treatment plan?
cited_learning_objective: Develop osteopathic treatment plan for blistering, ulcers, and trauma (PCPS 12,13, MK6)

options.rationale: These maneuvers add local trauma and do not constitute lymphatic techniques. They may worsen an ulcer.
Debridement is reserved for appropriate necrotic or infected tissue, while topical antibiotics may cause sensitization. Neither is the requested lymphatic pairing.
Reconstruction addresses arterial perfusion, while casting redistributes plantar pressure. They do not directly target lymphatic flow.
Peroxide can promote tissue breakdown, and dry exposure is less favorable for healing. These are not lymphatic techniques.
The pedal pump and treatment of the abdominal and pelvic diaphragms are components of the lymphatic-flow plan.

question: A 74-year-old woman has a mildly pruritic brown-red scaly plaque above the medial ankle. Varicosities, edema, and firm surrounding skin are present. She has no fever or tenderness. Which diagnosis best integrates the cutaneous findings and underlying mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Medial lower-leg scale, pigmentation, edema, varicosities, and fibrosis connect chronic venous hypertension with stasis dermatitis and lipodermatosclerosis.
Cellulitis is more acute and typically painful, erythematous, and associated with infection. Fever or acute tenderness would support it.
Erysipelas is an acute infectious process rather than a chronic pruritic scaly plaque. Acute systemic or painful findings would be needed.
Tinea corporis produces a sharply marginated annular eruption with central clearing. That morphology would make it appropriate.
Adult atopic dermatitis generally has a supporting childhood history and different distribution. Those findings are absent here.

question: A 52-year-old man has a shallow irregular ulcer near the medial malleolus with exudate and a weak pedal pulse. Which next step should be completed before initiating high external compression?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the ankle / brachial index (ABI) (MK2, PCPS6, SBP5)

options.rationale: This describes the correct test but does not specify calculation of the index; inference: the measurements would be used to calculate it. The more complete next step is obtaining the index.
The weak pulse raises concern for coexisting arterial disease, so the ABI should be determined before compression.
Topical antibiotics can cause contact sensitization and do not establish whether compression is safe. Evidence of infection would also be required.
Electrocautery adds trauma and may worsen the wound. It does not evaluate arterial perfusion.
Biopsy is unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear and the wound has not failed treatment. Diagnostic uncertainty or nonresponse would make it appropriate.

question: A 50-year-old man has a tender, shallow, irregular ulcer along the medial ankle with surrounding edema and pigmentation. His ankle-brachial index is 0.95. Which management plan is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.text: Dry exposure with daily peroxide cleansing
options.rationale: Air exposure and peroxide can impair healing and damage tissue. A moist dressing with saline cleansing is preferred.

options.text: Topical antibiotics with frequent dressing changes
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics increase sensitization risk, and frequent manipulation is unnecessary. Infection requiring systemic therapy would change management.
The findings indicate a venous ulcer, and the ABI does not meet the stated contraindication; moist primary dressing plus high compression addresses both wound and cause.
Casting redistributes plantar pressure in neuropathic ulcers. A plantar callus-associated lesion would support this plan.
This pairing does not fit uncomplicated venous ulcer care and debridement may worsen pyoderma gangrenosum. A rapidly expanding violaceous ulcer would change the approach.

question: A 61-year-old man who smokes reports exertional calf cramping and a painful distal leg wound. Examination shows a sharply demarcated pale base, minimal drainage, absent pedal pulse, and an ankle-brachial index of 0.6. Which next step should take priority?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Compression is contraindicated with the stated low ABI. Adequate arterial supply must be addressed first.
Topical steroids treat dermatitis or localized pyoderma therapy, not arterial hypoperfusion. An inflammatory dermatosis would be required.
Special footwear off-loads neuropathic plantar ulcers. A callus-associated plantar lesion with sensory loss would support it.
The ulcer and low ABI indicate arterial insufficiency; re-establishing adequate arterial supply through vascular evaluation takes priority.
Photography documents progress but does not correct severe perfusion impairment. Restoration of arterial flow is the priority.

question: A 58-year-old woman with diabetes has a plantar ulcer beneath a metatarsal head. The foot is warm with good color and palpable pulses, but sensation is decreased and a thick callus surrounds the wound. Which mechanism most directly initiated the lesion?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate between venous, arterial and neuropathic dermatologic manifestations (MK1,2 and PCPS5)

options.text: Venous valve failure causing superficial reflux
options.rationale: Venous reflux produces edema, pigmentation, and medial lower-leg ulceration. Those findings would be needed.
The warm foot and palpable pulses argue against dominant arterial insufficiency. Absent pulses and a pale punched-out lesion would support it.

options.text: Neutrophil influx causing rapid tissue breakdown
options.rationale: This mechanism produces pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid painful expansion with a violaceous undermined edge would support it.

options.text: Continuous pressure causing direct sacral necrosis
options.rationale: Sustained pressure causes pressure injuries, usually at immobilized support sites. The plantar callus and sensory loss indicate another pathway.
Loss of protective sensation permits repetitive unnoticed trauma, callus formation, and eventual plantar ulceration.

question: A 46-year-old man with long-standing diabetes has an ulcer beneath a plantar callus. A probe passes beneath surrounding intact skin but does not reach bone. Which next management step best addresses the primary mechanical contributor?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Debridement of surrounding callus plus restricted weight bearing, casting, or special footwear removes nonviable tissue and reduces repetitive plantar stress.
Compression and elevation primarily address venous hypertension. A medial ankle ulcer with edema would support that plan.
Arterial reconstruction is prioritized for ischemic ulcers. Absent pulses and a low ABI would make it appropriate.
Callus and nonviable tissue should be removed, but repeated aggressive trauma is not the primary pressure-control strategy and would be hazardous in pyoderma gangrenosum.
Peroxide and frequent manipulation can damage the wound. Gentle care and pressure redistribution are preferred.

question: A 63-year-old patient with diabetes has a plantar ulcer. Probing reveals a sinus extending to bone. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Compression treats venous insufficiency and does not address suspected bone infection. Venous ulcer features would be required.
Extension to bone raises concern for osteomyelitis; suspected cases should be admitted for evaluation and treatment.
Topical antibiotics are insufficient for suspected bone involvement and can cause sensitization. A superficial localized issue would be required.
Pulse loss is not required before acting on suspected osteomyelitis. Bone extension already warrants escalation.
Off-loading remains useful but is inadequate when bone involvement is suspected. Hospital evaluation is required.

question: A 72-year-old immobile patient has intact sacral skin with persistent redness that does not blanch. Which intervention is the next best step?
cited_learning_objective: List preventative care for stasis dermatitis and the various forms of leg and sacral ulcers (PCPS 10,11)

options.rationale: No full-thickness necrosis is present. Debridement becomes relevant for appropriate stage III or IV injuries.
Compression addresses venous disease, not an early pressure injury. A venous lower-leg ulcer would be required.
Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin is stage I; immediate pressure relief, repositioning, and support surfaces help prevent progression.
Peroxide can increase tissue injury. The intact skin primarily requires pressure relief rather than traumatic cleansing.

options.text: Probe deeply for underlying bone involvement
options.rationale: There is no open ulcer to probe. Probing is used when evaluating an open diabetic foot ulcer for undermining or bone extension.

question: An elderly hospitalized patient with immobility and urinary leakage develops a sacral crater extending through the skin into subcutaneous tissue without exposed fascia, muscle, or bone. Which classification is most accurate?
cited_learning_objective: Utilizing history and physical exam stage a sacral ulcer. (PCPS 2,3,7)

options.rationale: Stage I retains intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Intact skin would be required.
Stage II is partial-thickness loss or a blister. The described full-thickness crater is deeper.
Stage IV reaches muscle, bone, tendon, joint capsule, or other supporting structures. Such involvement is absent.
Full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue without involvement of underlying fascia or deeper structures defines stage III.
Impending ulceration refers to intact non-blanchable skin rather than an established full-thickness crater.

question: A 50-year-old woman with inflammatory bowel disease develops intensely painful lesions that begin as pustules and enlarge over four days into ulcers with undermined violaceous edges. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Trauma can worsen pyoderma gangrenosum through pathergy. Debridement is appropriate for selected necrotic or infected pressure and venous wounds instead.
Compression targets venous hypertension. A medial lower-leg ulcer with edema and an acceptable ABI would support it.
Topical antibiotics can cause sensitization and do not treat the neutrophilic process. A proven superficial infection would change management.

options.text: Observe for six weeks before referral
options.rationale: This rapidly progressive painful disorder is a dermatologic emergency. Six-week observation applies to nonresponsive venous ulcers.
Rapid painful ulceration with an undermined violaceous border suggests pyoderma gangrenosum, which requires urgent dermatologic evaluation.

question: A rapidly expanding painful ulcer worsens after attempted debridement. Biopsy shows no specific diagnostic pattern, and infection is excluded. Which mechanism best explains the deterioration?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Pyoderma gangrenosum is mediated by dermal neutrophilic inflammation and may worsen after trauma through pathergy.
Arterial ulcers reflect impaired perfusion and delayed healing, not trauma-induced neutrophilic expansion. Low ABI and absent pulses would support arterial disease.
Compression treats rather than causes venous hypertension when arterial supply is adequate. Venous reflux arises from valve incompetence.
Callus reflects repetitive neuropathic pressure, not lymphatic valve destruction. A plantar sensory-deficient foot would support callus-mediated ulceration.
A moist environment generally promotes wound healing. It does not explain trauma-associated rapid ulcer expansion.

question: A 27-year-old man has recurrent painful perianal abscesses and draining sinus tracts for 16 months. There are no gastrointestinal symptoms and no axillary lesions. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Acne conglobata predominantly affects the back, chest, and face and was contrasted as lacking this sinus-tract pattern. Those locations would support it.
Chronic painful inflammation with abscesses and draining sinuses in an apocrine-bearing perianal region supports hidradenitis suppurativa.
Cutaneous Crohn disease would be supported by a fistula extending past the dentate line and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Granuloma inguinale presents with genital ulceration rather than chronic perianal abscesses and sinus tracts. Genital ulcers would support it.
Lymphogranuloma venereum was associated with unilateral groin involvement rather than this chronic localized sinus-tract disease.

question: A patient with chronic perianal inflammatory nodules and draining tracts has years of persistent disease. Which long-term complication warrants particular surveillance?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Basal cell transformation was not the malignant complication linked to chronic hidradenitis. A different disease association would be required.
Melanoma was not identified as the transformation risk of hidradenitis. A pigmented neoplastic process would be needed.
Chronic hidradenitis suppurativa carries a stated risk of malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma.
Venous sarcoma was not associated with the chronic inflammatory sinus tracts described. Venous disease instead causes dermatitis, fibrosis, and ulceration.
Neutrophilic lymphoma was not identified as a complication. Neutrophilic influx pertains to pyoderma gangrenosum rather than this malignancy.

question: A patient with chronic venous disease develops markedly rough, pebbled, hyperkeratotic lower-leg skin after recurrent inflammation of draining vessels. Which mechanism best explains this progression?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.text: Sensory loss with repetitive plantar trauma
options.rationale: This mechanism produces neuropathic callus and plantar ulceration. Decreased sensation at a pressure point would support it.
Arterial obstruction produces absent pulses, ischemic skin, and punched-out ulcers. It does not explain pebbled lymphatic skin.
This mechanism describes pyoderma gangrenosum. Rapid painful ulcer expansion after trauma would support it.
Inflammation can damage draining lymphatics, producing lymphatic insufficiency and the pebbled hyperkeratotic skin of elephantiasis verrucosa nostra.
Sustained pressure can cause deep pressure injury. Immobility with full-thickness tissue destruction would be required.

question: A patient with a medial ankle ulcer begins appropriate compression, elevation, moist dressings, and dermatitis treatment. After six weeks, serial measurements show no decrease in wound size. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the clinical features of the underlying mechanism of disease, and basic treatments for stasis dermatitis & ulcers, venous insufficiency, lipodermatosclerosis and other common related dermatologic conditions (MK 1,2, PCPS 7,10)

options.rationale: Failure to reduce in size after six weeks meets the stated threshold for referral rather than indefinite unchanged care.
Hydrogen peroxide can cause skin breakdown and does not address treatment failure. Saline cleansing remains preferred.
Topical antibiotics can produce contact dermatitis and are not indicated without infection. Sensitization could further delay healing.
A moist wound environment promotes healing. Dry exposure does not address the lack of response.
A venous ulcer that does not shrink after six weeks of treatment should be referred to dermatology or a wound care clinic.

question: A 68-year-old patient has lower-leg edema, varicosities, hyperpigmentation, and an exudative medial ankle ulcer. The ankle-brachial index is 0.65. Which management modification is required?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the ankle / brachial index (ABI) (MK2, PCPS6, SBP5)

options.rationale: Although the ulcer has venous features, an ABI below 0.8 indicates significant arterial disease and contraindicates compression.
Increasing compression despite an ABI below 0.8 conflicts with the stated safety threshold. An ABI of at least 0.8 would be needed.
Prophylactic topical antibiotics can cause contact sensitization. Clinical infection would require appropriate infection management.
Hydrogen peroxide may cause tissue breakdown. Saline is the recommended cleanser.
Moist primary dressings promote healing better than air exposure. Drying does not correct the arterial contraindication.
